flashcards.q: What is the single precondition that makes a linear sweep sufficient to merge overlapping intervals?
flashcards.a: The intervals must be sorted by start value first. Once sorted, if interval k doesn't overlap the current merged block, no later interval can either, since all later starts are >= start[k].

flashcards.q: When merging interval [start,end] into a running merged block, why must you take max(merged.end, end) instead of overwriting with end?
flashcards.a: The new interval might be fully nested inside the merged block (e.g. [2,3] inside [1,10]); overwriting with its smaller end would silently shrink the merged block and corrupt the result.

flashcards.q: For Non-Overlapping Intervals (LC435, minimize removals), which field do you sort by, and why is this different from the base merge problem?
flashcards.a: Sort by END time, not start. The greedy 'keep the earliest-ending compatible interval' proof (activity selection / exchange argument) only holds when sorted by end; sorting by start can pick a long early interval that blocks several short ones.

flashcards.q: How do you solve Meeting Rooms II (minimum rooms needed) without a merge step at all?
flashcards.a: It's a concurrency count, not a merge: sort by start, use a min-heap of active end times, pop entries whose end <= current start (room freed), push the current end; the heap's peak size across the sweep is the answer.

flashcards.q: What is the sweep-line alternative to the min-heap solution for Meeting Rooms II, and what does it compute?
flashcards.a: Create +1 events at each meeting start and -1 events at each meeting end, sort all events by time, sweep while tracking a running sum; the maximum value the running sum reaches is the minimum rooms needed.

flashcards.q: Why does Insert Interval (LC57) not need a full O(n log n) re-sort even though it changes the interval set?
flashcards.a: The input is already sorted and merged. A single O(n) linear scan suffices: copy intervals ending before the new one starts, absorb all overlapping intervals into the new one's expanding bounds, then copy the rest.

flashcards.q: In Interval List Intersections (LC986), after emitting an intersection, which pointer do you advance, and why?
flashcards.a: Advance whichever interval has the SMALLER end value. It has been fully 'used up' against everything it could intersect going forward since both lists are sorted by start; advancing the other pointer risks skipping a still-relevant interval.

flashcards.q: How do you compute Employee Free Time from multiple employees' individually-sorted schedules?
flashcards.a: Flatten all schedules into one list, run the base merge across the union, then every gap between consecutive merged blocks (where next.start > current.end) is a free-time interval.

flashcards.q: What is the overall time complexity of the base Merge Intervals algorithm, and what step dominates it?
flashcards.a: O(n log n) total, entirely dominated by the initial sort by start; the linear sweep that actually merges overlapping blocks contributes only an O(n) lower-order term.

flashcards.q: Why can a naive per-insertion re-merge of a streaming interval set (LC352, Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals) become O(n^2 log n) overall, and what avoids it?
flashcards.a: Re-sorting and re-merging the entire structure from scratch on every single insertion costs O(n log n) per insertion across n insertions. A balanced-BST/TreeMap-based structure avoids this by merging only the newly inserted value's immediate neighbors, not the whole set.
